I think it's less about long term stories, though I don't entirely disagree, but a lot more to do with American wrestling being very 2D in terms of emotional storytelling. 

The major independent promotion had had characters who are very multifaceted in terms of their character whether it's the current portrayal of this developing storyline of him botching against an opponent and working it into a storyline that isn't entirely front and center every week.

Hell the stable plot line has had a lot of this too, the lower ranked wrestlers aren't just joining the group because their jobbers and no one cares what we do with them but we actually get a motivation to help make us care a little more about why jobbers are joining this team.

Also just to be clear not saying the promotion is some great storytelling company, guys like the top heel and the top face are still very classic heels and faces who just go out and do the schtick you'd expect, though they're both phenomenal talkers. But compared to the major corporate promotion promos it feels way less stilted and impersonal in the independent promotion.

Food writing is just like any other type of pop-media writing whether it's movies, technology, music, etc.

You have your "high" and "low" forms. (Pop vs Orchestra, Marvel vs Martin Scorsese movies, etc.) and in food that's often the difference between the local small restaurant serving up burgers and fries and a 2-3 star Michelin restaurant. 

And part of the issue is the inherent snobbery that comes with these sorts of things and when you're trying to appeal to the high-end of the spectrum you tend to be railroaded into "talking smart" and trying to sound as verbose and wordy as you can manage.

It's like the difference between Guy Ferari or even someone like Anthony Bourdain (RIP) where they may occasionally be wordy with their reviews of food but they usually keep things simple (or go overly simple in Guy's case).

Compared to someone who presents themselves as being high-brow "real foodie" type presenters who focus on the buzzwords and using as many fancy sounding big words as they can to make someone feel smart while consuming their media.

It's not a dig at the person themselves, I think Morroco is great on screen, it's just that he's very much that high-brow food type of person while someone like Brad is more of the Diners Drive Ins and Dives type of every man personality where he usually says things in the simplest way he can, even if he's talking about something your average american chef has no idea about like Sumac.
